ateret-zekenim/1:_: It is forbidden to say "this meat is for Passover," but meat of fish and fowl is permitted (my teacher in the Bach). And some forbid [even] a chicken (Maharil). And if one said "this meat is for Passover," it is forbidden to eat it and even for benefit it is forbidden, and it requires burial because it appears as though one consecrated consecrated items outside [the Temple]. Nevertheless, regarding chickens one does not forbid b'dieved, because it is only a stringency l'chatchila; so it appears to me from the words of the Talmud.
chatam-sofer/1:_: In the Mechaber: forbidden to say regarding any animal. It appears to me, see responsa Chatam Sofer Orach Chayyim siman 139 [regarding a certain youth who had a milk lamb in his flock and said to his uncle "this is my Paschal offering," and after they raised an outcry about this the youth apologized that he knew nothing of the matter of consecration and they only spoke in jest and mockery and the talk of youths. And in his responsum he first explains the matter in Pesachim daf 50b, and wrote that according to this, what he said — "this lamb shall be a Paschal offering" — is consecrated for everyone. And afterward he wrote that if one believes him that it was jest, it is possible it is not a claim at all as he explains there. Therefore one should ask about his vow on Passover and regret — except that it is difficult to permit the prohibition of the stringency of consecrated items through a question and opening of a sage in this time, who are lenient in permitting vows and do not wish to understand what is explained to them how they should regret; therefore it appears to me to devise another combined remedy for permitting that vow — namely, after his vow was already permitted, he should command a minor gentile who does not exchange with an adult Jew, and cause a blemish in it fit to permit it through three members of the congregation as with a firstborn; and afterward stand it before a court and they shall assess its monetary value and redeem it and cast it into the river; and a kohen is not required, as stated in Sanhedrin daf 15a. And in any case, since it is good, there is no loss that the assessor be a kohen; and see there well in the entire responsum].
chokhmat-shlomo/1:_: Section 1: Forbidden to say regarding any animal, whether living or slaughtered, "this meat for Passover." It appears to me: I saw in the Yerushalmi chapter "How do we roast," halacha 1: they bring in a calf mekulas on the first night of Yom Tov of Passover, but not a kid mekulas — end of his words. And the Korban HaEdah there wondered, for in the chapter "In a place where they practiced" it is explicit that even calf meat is forbidden, and so ruled all the decisors, and he left it "this requires further study." And in truth it is difficult for me, for it is in the manner of what is stated in Shas in Chullin that fowl goes up on the table with cheese and is not eaten, and Beit Shammai say it does not go up and is not eaten; and it is explicit there in Shas that they disagree whether we decree a decree upon a decree or not. And accordingly, here too the intention is thus: certainly to eat — even calf meat is forbidden, for we decree on account of a kid, since its prohibition is weighty; if, since its commandment is that day — so when the Temple stood one should decree more, and therefore they decreed even a decree upon a decree. But to bring in and not to eat — if a kid mekulas, we decree bringing on account of eating, and in this we decree a decree upon a decree; but a calf to bring in, which is three decrees — we do not decree; therefore to bring in alone, a calf mekulas is permitted. And what it cited at the beginning the language "they bring a kid" on the night of Yom Tov — that is because of the seifa that specifically it is bringing and not eating; it also cited the beginning "they bring." And in the chapter "In a place where they practiced," which deals with eating — here even a calf mekulas is forbidden; and this resolves it, and it is clear and correct; understand well.
eliyah-rabbah/1:_: [1] Forbidden, etc. And if one said, one forbids benefit — if not in a chicken; and the mind of Olah Tamid is always to permit even in eating, even in making mekulas; and so he brought proof in Chok Yaakov that Rambam ruled chapter 14 of Laws of Sacrifices as R' Shimon, who is stringent in Shas [Pesachim] daf 13, and in Sifrei Yoreh De'ah siman 5 it will be explained.
kaf-hachayyim/1:_: (1) [Section 1] Forbidden to say, etc. And if one said "this meat for Passover," it is forbidden to eat it; and even for benefit it is forbidden and requires burial (Bach, Or Zarua, and so too Peri Chadash). And he wrote that so is frequent in the book of Damascus Eliezer in tractate Chullin daf 77a, see there. And Magen Avraham note 2: to distinguish — in a kid and lamb one should be stringent b'dieved, and in other meat one should not be stringent, see there. And so inclined Chok Yosef section 3, and so too Chayei Adam general 131 section 8. However in Orach Chayyim daf 77a section 11 he wrote in the name of R' Shimon the purchaser: one should not say "this for Passover," for it appears as consecrating for the name of Passover; and if he said, it is permitted to eat, see there. And so too Taz note 1: if one transgressed and said, b'dieved there is no prohibition of eating, see there. And so too Eliyah Rabbah section 1, and so is the opinion of the rabbi Mekor Chayyim on daf 173b, that if he said, b'dieved it is permitted, see there. And so in responsa Knesset Yechezkel siman 18 he expanded to prove as the opinion of Taz and Shach that b'dieved it is permitted in eating, see there; and so agreed Chayei Adam section 1, Birkat Yosef section 1, Ma'amar Mordechai section 2, and so is the opinion of Nahar Shalom section 1, Laws of Passover section 1, Magen HaElef section 2; and so too R' Zalman section 2, that b'dieved even if one said on a living kid and lamb "this meat for Passover," they are permitted in eating, even if he said so verbally after midnight — because of mar'it ha'ayin one does not forbid b'dieved — end of his words; except that he wrote there in a gloss that in a kid and lamb it is good to be concerned for the opinion of the stringent and forbid in eating specifically when there is no great need and not a time of distress, see there. And in any case, this is simple: unspecified vows are to be stringent and their explanation is to be lenient; and we also require mouth and heart equal, as written in Yoreh De'ah siman 210 and siman 211; therefore one should ask him, and if he says his intention is only for the Festival of Passover, then one may permit.
shaarei-teshuvah/1:_: Bahma, Abhat and A. MS. 13 in the Bechash in Pesachim Tidhushedi, page 13, which he wrote to Yashav, Ko. B. B. and A., who wrote Degadi Mekols. There is no prohibition 21 to eat it on the nights of Passover, which is seen in the name of Pesach Kakhil Lia and Ei Shabik Lia for tomorrow and on the following day. And look at the Sh. C. H. Dafilo saying that when slaughtering for the sake of Passover, it is permitted from Daoriyata only from Durbanan Asor 18 and the T. Sh. S. 12 per the 16th and 16th Shach:
yad-ephraim/1:_: In Magen Avraham note 2: that they will say one consecrated it for the monetary value of Passover — meaning, according to Rashi the reason is not because we say one already consecrated it, but that we are concerned it will appear as though he is consecrating it now; and if so, in slaughtered meat there is no room to say one consecrates it now for Passover, and one must say it appears as consecrating it for the monetary value of Passover; and according to this reason all animals are forbidden; and on this Magen Avraham wrote to answer what was asked of the Beit Yosef, etc. And his words "this requires further study" — in my humble opinion they are reconciled: regarding a living animal it fits well that there is concern, since if we say one consecrated it for the monetary value of Passover, it has no redemption — which is not so in slaughtered meat, which is comparable to other matters of monetary holiness and has redemption. And although in Shulchan Aruch he cited that one consecrated it while alive, nevertheless according to Rashi from the Torah one should be concerned for this; in truth it is said: since he eats it, presumably he did not make a prohibition, but he consecrated it now and it is only monetary holiness and he redeemed it. And it appears to me the Mechaber cited the stringency of both — Rashi and Tosafos — and we are concerned the viewer will say one consecrated it while alive for the monetary value of Passover; and therefore even slaughtered meat from other animals is forbidden. And nevertheless "this requires further study": from where do we know this reasoning? Perhaps the Tosafos do not hold it appears as though one consecrated it while alive, but because the reasoning of Rashi — that one consecrated it for its monetary value — is not reasonable to them; and since this appears from things one consecrated, they will think one consecrated it while alive; but anything we need to say one consecrated for the monetary value of Passover — from the Torah they will rely to say one consecrated it now for the monetary value of Passover, and he may well eat it through redemption; and "this requires further study."
